resources.string: Follow the system setting, or force light or dark.
Derive the palette from your wallpaper instead of using the MultiStore palette.
The language of the interface. Store listings stay in the language of their source.
Couldn\'t save the setting. Try again.

Install even when the checksum the store publishes doesn\'t match the downloaded file. Better left off: a mismatch means the file isn\'t the one the store described. When on, the app installs but the verification card says “hash not verified”.

Install even when the APK isn\'t signed with the key the store declared. It doesn\'t cover an app already installed with a different key: Android refuses that update anyway, and the only way out is to uninstall and reinstall, losing its data — a choice MultiStore offers you app by app, with this switch off too.
Download store catalogues and app files over mobile data as well. A full F‑Droid catalogue is about 18 MB. When off, MultiStore asks before starting.
When a store asks for a check

Some stores answer with a check that a browser passes on its own, with no captcha and nothing to tap. MultiStore can run it in a hidden browser view: the page is really executed, never faked. Choose how far the app may go by itself.
When a store asks for a check
Run it in a hidden view
Run it, and keep trying longer
Never open a store page for me to tap

Two stores hand over their file only after a real tap on their own page. MultiStore opens that page inside the app, so the file still goes through every check before it is installed. Turn this on and those downloads are no longer offered.
Allow ads in the store page

The assisted download opens the store’s own page, where ads are the most common way malware is served. MultiStore drops requests to known advertising and tracking hosts. Cloudflare and reCAPTCHA are never dropped, so turning this on does not unblock a download that stalls on a challenge.

Compacts the catalogue database and empties its write log. It deletes nothing you can see: the catalogue, your installed apps and your settings all stay. A full F-Droid sync leaves the database around 65 MB.
Nothing to reclaim: the database is already compact.
Which stores MultiStore searches. Turning one off hides it from results and stops every request to it.
Temporarily unreachable — MultiStore will try again on its own.
Responding, but its pages have changed: results may be incomplete.
Free and open-source apps only. Publishes a signed catalogue, a checksum for every version and the signing key it expects, so a download can be verified end to end.
Mirrors apps from Google Play. Publishes no checksums: MultiStore can confirm the package name matches, not that the file is the one the listing described.
Human-reviewed mirror with a no-piracy policy. Publishes the checksum and the signing certificate of each file, so downloads are verified as thoroughly as F-Droid\'s.

Modified builds — premium features unlocked. Publishes the package name but no checksum, and a modified build is signed by whoever modified it: MultiStore can confirm which app you are installing, not that nobody changed it along the way.
General mirror with a published checksum for every file, so downloads are verified end to end. The file itself is behind a human check: MultiStore opens the store page and you tap Download.
How often MultiStore looks for newer versions of the apps you installed from here.
Postpone the automatic check until the device is plugged in.
Only applies to the automatic check, which is off.
Fetch the APK as soon as an update is found, so installing is one tap. On a metered connection the download waits, unless you allowed it under Network.

Also offer beta, alpha and release candidate builds, where a store publishes them. Applies to a first install and to updates alike. To take just one preview build once, open Previous versions on the app page instead.
Download and install without asking. Everything is verified exactly as it is when you tap Install yourself.
Needs Shizuku or root. Without one, Android has to ask you before every install, and it cannot ask while the app is in the background.
Keep checking, but do not post a notification. Available updates are still listed on the home screen.
Who writes the package to the system. The system confirmation always works; Shizuku and root install without asking, if you have them.
Permission not granted. MultiStore will keep using the system confirmation.

MultiStore downloads a small signed file with the selectors and addresses it uses to read each store, so a store that changes its pages can be fixed without a new app version. Turn this on to keep only what shipped with the app.
Using the configuration that shipped with the app.

resources.string: Ask now instead of waiting for the next scheduled check. Whatever arrives is used from the next start.
Off, results leave out what a store labels as adult. Only one of the stores labels it at all, and it labels it incompletely: this hides what the store declares, not everything it carries.

Modified builds, with the best metadata of any modded source and the worst binaries: about one file in four is gone and answers with a server error, so MultiStore checks the file exists before it starts. Publishes the package name via the Google Play link, but no checksum. It is also the only store that labels adult content, which is what the NSFW switch acts on.

Modified and unmodified builds side by side. Publishes no package name anywhere on the site, so MultiStore cannot confirm which app an install actually is — matching relies on title and developer alone. Some files do carry a checksum, and where they do the download is verified end to end.

Modified builds — «Money Mod», «Mod Menu», «Premium» — alongside unmodified ones, and a large catalogue of old versions. Publishes no checksum anywhere, so a download can be checked only against the package name, which it does publish for most apps. The file is behind a page you open yourself and tap: watch out, that page also carries advertisements shaped exactly like the download button.

Modified builds — «MOD», «Premium», «Paid» — and, on some pages, the unmodified file from Google Play right beside them. Publishes no checksum anywhere, so a download can be checked only against the package name, which it does publish for most apps. Search returns at most 60 results, whatever the query. Its own files sit behind a one-click page; the original ones sit on a separate host that is sometimes gone.
Refuse the app index we publish
The Home shows “Most popular” and “What’s new” from an index we sign and publish. Turn this on and the app stops downloading it: the Home keeps the local catalogue, and nothing else changes.
MultiStore is not on any store, so a new version is announced in the same index. A downloaded update goes through the same checks as any other app, including the signature comparison.
How long to wait for a store

Stores do not answer together: one reads a local index in milliseconds, another waits three seconds before it is even polite to ask. A store that runs out of time is listed as missing next to the results of the others — the search is not held up for it.
How long to wait for a store
No setting contains those words. Try a single word, or clear the field to see everything again.
Say when a file MultiStore fetched is ready
Only for downloads MultiStore starts on its own. A file you asked for shows its progress on the app page, so there is nothing a notification would add.
Say how an unattended install went
Only for installs MultiStore performs on its own. The case worth reading is the failure: an update refused because the signature changed never comes back on its own.
Say when a store did not answer

Only for the periodic check, where the stores polled are exactly the ones your installed apps update from — so a silent store means apps that quietly stop updating. During a search the missing store is already named next to the results.

MultiStore always records what goes wrong. Turn this on and it also records what goes right: the full address of every request, the response code and how long it took. Addresses include your search terms on the stores that put them in the path. It stays on this device and leaves only where you export it.

Writes a text file with the app version, this device, the state of each store, the configuration in use and the recorded events. Read it before you send it: with the switch above on it also contains the addresses MultiStore requested.
The report could not be saved.
How results are ordered until you change it for one search. Only three criteria are offered: every store publishes a title, three publish a rating, and none publishes a date on every row.
Whether search starts on apps, games or both. Only one store labels its listings, so with a type selected the others are left out of the search and named under the results.

App pages, versions and screenshots saved on this device, plus the full local index of stores that publish one. Emptying it frees the most space and costs the most to rebuild: F-Droid alone is about 18 MB to download again. Your installed apps, their update channels and your cross-store choices are kept.
Installer files still on this device: downloads you never installed, and anything kept by the setting below. Transfers still in progress or paused are left alone.
App icons and screenshots. They come back on their own the next time you scroll a list.
Raw pages kept so that going back to a result you just saw does not ask the store again. Emptying this costs one extra request per page you revisit.

Search will find nothing on stores with a local index until it has been downloaded again — about 18 MB for F-Droid, on whatever connection you are on then. Your installed apps and their update channels are kept.

Off, the installer file is deleted as soon as the install succeeds. On, it stays and is reused: installing that same version again costs no download. It also means the space above keeps growing, and the button that empties it is the only thing that shrinks it.

A page is refetched when the store\'s own freshness window runs out; this is how long the old copy is kept afterwards, so that reopening yesterday\'s search shows something instantly. It does not touch stores with a local index: theirs is a catalogue you asked to download, not a page that went stale.
How much disk icons and screenshots may use. Takes effect the next time the app starts, because the size is fixed when the cache is opened.
Android has to be told that MultiStore may install apps. It is a system setting, so it can be revoked from outside the app — including by a system update.
This device has no screen for that setting: the %1$s software may have moved or removed it. Look for “install unknown apps” in the system settings.
MultiStore is free, has no ads and sends nothing anywhere. If it is useful to you, a contribution helps keep it going. It opens in your browser.
Offer to install as soon as it is downloaded

When a download finishes and you have already left the app page, MultiStore opens the system\'s installation prompt on its own. Off, the file waits for you in Downloads. It can interrupt what you are doing in the app, and it never applies to files fetched by the automatic update check with installing turned off.
Not needed with the installer you chose: it installs without asking anything.
How many finished downloads the Downloads screen remembers: installed, failed, and deleted. Transfers in progress and files waiting to be installed are never counted, and never removed.
It removes the installer files still on this device. Transfers in progress or paused are left alone.
